findings.paper_title: 07 - Audit progress report; regaining assurance progress report; and sector update_Final
findings.headline: No audit assurance over opening balances or closing reserves for 2025/26
findings.detail: The auditor has no assurance over opening balances for 2025/26 and no assurance over closing reserves due to uncertainty over opening amounts. Recovery plan focuses only on in-year transactions, with reserves rebuild described as 'challenging' to achieve before April 2028 LGR.
findings.matters: Absence of assurance over reserves means the council's true financial position and available reserves are unknown, making it impossible to assess financial flexibility or genuine debt capacity.
findings.figures: Recovery timeline extends to April 2028; reserves rebuild not expected to complete before Local Government Reorganisation vesting day
findings.quote: we have no assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; and No assurance over the closing reserves balance also due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Audit progress report; regaining assurance progress report; and sector update_Final
findings.headline: Significant weakness in Value for Money arrangements persists from prior year
findings.detail: A significant weakness in the council's close-down and financial reporting process within governance arrangements was identified in 2024/25 and continues in 2025/26, indicating structural governance problems remain unresolved.
findings.matters: A persistent VfM significant weakness means the council's financial management and governance processes remain materially inadequate, creating governance risk for lenders.
findings.figures: Weakness identified in consecutive years (2024/25 and 2025/26)
findings.quote: In line with the prior year, we have identified a significant weakness in the Council's close-down and financial reporting process within the governance arrangements, based on our risk assessment procedures.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Audit progress report; regaining assurance progress report; and sector update_Final
findings.headline: Finance team capacity constraints identified as primary driver of persistent audit failures
findings.detail: The auditor concluded that audit issues are 'primarily driven by capacity constraints within the finance team, alongside limitations in accounting systems'. Training delivered in May-June 2025 did not result in sustained improvements despite management's willingness and ambition.
findings.matters: Insufficient finance team capacity means financial reporting reliability cannot be assured without structural changes to staffing or systems, creating ongoing audit and operational risk.
findings.figures: Two training sessions delivered (May-June 2025); £46,661 grant funding provided for build-back support
findings.quote: We have concluded that these issues are primarily driven by capacity constraints within the finance team, alongside limitations in accounting systems and processes in producing auditable information without significant manual intervention.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Audit progress report; regaining assurance progress report; and sector update_Final
findings.headline: Auditor anticipates issuing a disclaimer of opinion for 2025/26 financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor expects to disclaim the opinion on 2025/26 accounts due to absence of assurance over opening balances. This continues a five-year pattern from 2020/21 to 2024/25 where all opinions were disclaimed under backstop arrangements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means no audit assurance on the council's financial position, eliminating the primary verification that financial statements are reliable for lenders assessing credit risk.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2020/21 to 2024/25); 2025/26 expected to follow
findings.quote: Due to the absence of assurance over opening balances and inability to build back assurance during 2025/26, we anticipate issuing a disclaimer of opinion for the 2025/26 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix A - SDC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Eight audits remain in progress at report date, delaying completion of 2025-26 audit plan and 2026-27 assurance opinion
findings.detail: Eight audit engagements were still ongoing at the time the report was drafted: Revenues & Benefits Partnership Review, Cyber Security, Disaster Recovery, Capital Budget Monitoring, Corporate Governance, Corporate Complaints, Asset Management, and Licensing HUB. The report notes that carry-forward of engagements from 2024-25 has resulted in slippage in 2025-26 planned deliverables.
findings.matters: Audit plan slippage delays assurance delivery and means the council does not have timely assurance over key control areas like capital budget monitoring, cyber security, and revenues & benefits.
findings.figures: 8 audits in progress at time of drafting; carried forward from 2024-25 resulted in slippage
findings.quote: As indicated in the table, the carry forward of audit engagements from 2024-25 has resulted in some slippage in the 2025-26 planned deliverables, with 8 audits in progress at the time of drafting this report.

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix A - SDC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Performance Management audit found services are not linking objectives to the Council Plan or measuring outcomes
findings.detail: The Performance Management audit found that although the council has a sound framework, services do not consistently use it. Critically, there is no link between service objectives and the Council Plan, no link between objectives and performance indicators, most indicators are output-based rather than outcome-based, and almost half of all performance indicators do not directly contribute to a specific Council Plan theme. This means the council lacks visibility into whether services are actually delivering strategic priorities.
findings.matters: If services cannot demonstrate they are delivering against council strategy and measuring outcomes, the council cannot effectively manage performance or justify spending decisions to stakeholders or audit.
findings.figures: Almost half of performance indicators do not directly contribute to a specific Council Plan theme
findings.quote: However, services do not consistently use the templates as intended, meaning they are ineffective in practice. Nor do they link their objectives within their service plan to the Council Plan or Corporate Strategy, meaning the golden thread is seemingly unapparent. Additionally, there is no link within the service plan template between service objectives and performance indicators, so it is unclear which indicators relate to which objectives and how they sufficiently measure performance.

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix A - SDC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Two ongoing fraud investigations remain unresolved at time of report
findings.detail: Internal Audit initiated investigations into two matters relating to potential fraud during 2025-26. These remain ongoing and unresolved at the time the report was drafted in July 2026.
findings.matters: Unresolved fraud investigations indicate active integrity issues within the council that could affect financial controls and governance.
findings.figures: 2 fraud investigations initiated and ongoing
findings.quote: During 2025-26 investigations were initiated into two matters relating to potential fraud – these remain ongoing at the time of drafting this report.

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix A - SDC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion
findings.headline: 48 audit actions remain outstanding from prior years, including 9 High priority actions not yet implemented
findings.detail: The follow-up table shows significant numbers of actions carried forward without implementation. High priority items (9), Medium priority items (30), and Low priority items (9) remain outstanding. The report notes that management requests deferrals when unable to implement by agreed dates, and Internal Audit is working to reduce deferral numbers.
findings.matters: Outstanding audit recommendations indicate the council is not implementing agreed improvements to its control systems on schedule, suggesting management may lack capacity or priority clarity to address identified risks.
findings.figures: Total carried forward to 2025-26: 48 actions (9 High, 30 Medium, 9 Low)
findings.quote: When a service is unable to implement actions by the agreed date, they can request a deferral. Deferrals are agreed for valid reasons though the original risks do of course remain until implementation is complete. Internal Audit continues to work with Strategic Management to reduce the numbers of deferrals

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix A - SDC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Two audits received Limited assurance, indicating significant control gaps in Performance Management and Business Continuity
findings.detail: Performance Management received Limited assurance because services do not consistently use the council's performance management templates, there is no clear link between service objectives and the Council Plan, and most performance indicators measure outputs rather than outcomes. Business Continuity similarly received Limited assurance. These are areas where improvement is required to manage risks effectively.
findings.matters: Limited assurance audits indicate significant gaps in governance or control systems that could affect the council's ability to manage key business functions and risks.
findings.figures: 2 of 11 assurance-rated audits received Limited assurance (Performance Management and Business Continuity)
findings.quote: Of the 11 assurance rated audits, 3 audits completed have received Substantial and a further 6 received Reasonable assurance which indicates that the control framework is generally operating well. Two audits (Business Continuity and Performance Management) received Limited assurance.

findings.paper_title: 09 annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: New governance issue: potential member conflicts of interest in Community Asset Transfer bids.
findings.detail: The council has identified a new governance issue where members sit on both authorities involved in particular Community Asset Transfer bids, creating potential conflicts of interest in decision-making.
findings.matters: Unresolved conflicts of interest in asset decisions create reputational and legal risk, and undermine the integrity of the governance framework that a lender relies on to trust council decision-making.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The new governance issue highlighted in this AGS is due to potential member conflicts of interest regarding bids for Community Asset Transfers as some members serve on both authorities involved in a particular bid.

findings.paper_title: 09 annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating ongoing operational and governance strain.
findings.detail: The council is managing a Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) process while attempting to maintain business-as-usual delivery. This is explicitly identified as a governance challenge, the second of three issues, suggesting the reorganisation is creating competing demands on management capacity and focus.
findings.matters: Major organisational restructuring typically diverts management attention and resources from financial management and service delivery; a lender would want to understand whether LGR disruption is affecting the council's operational stability.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The second relates to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) with the challenge to continue to deliver business as usual whilst meeting the demands and priorities of LGR.

findings.paper_title: 09 annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Financial reporting and closedown arrangements identified as a governance weakness.
findings.detail: The council has previously highlighted and continues to work on strengthening its closedown and financial reporting arrangements. This is explicitly identified as one of three governance issues facing the council, suggesting control weaknesses in the year-end financial process.
findings.matters: Financial reporting control failures directly undermine the accuracy and timeliness of accounts, and affect a lender's confidence in the council's financial position and management capability.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The first is regarding strengthening the closedown and financial reporting arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: The pay award for April 2025 cost £256,000 more than budgeted and required supplementary funding from reserves
findings.detail: The council's pay award provision was exceeded by £256,000, forcing a supplementary estimate from the Budget Stabilisation Reserve. This is a broad-based cost pressure affecting all services and signals either understated pay inflation assumptions or higher-than-expected award levels.
findings.matters: A lender will see this as evidence that the council's budget assumptions for workforce costs are not holding. If pay awards continue to exceed budget, payroll costs will become a structural pressure.
findings.figures: £256,000 unfavourable variance
findings.quote: Pay award 2025 – as explained above, the April 2025 pay award was forecast to be £256,000 above budget.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: The capital programme spent only £8.1m of £11.3m budget, a 28% underspend driven by works rephasing and Better Care Fund underperformance
findings.detail: The council budgeted £11.3m for capital but delivered only £8.1m. The slippage is attributed to rephasing of work at Farmstead Drive (deferred to later 2026) and underspends on the Better Care Fund. This pattern of underspend suggests either optimistic budgeting, slower-than-expected project delivery, or restricted funding.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's capital investment capacity and delivery track record will flag a 28% slippage as material. It could indicate poor project management, external funding delay, or that capital budgets are not realistic.
findings.figures: £3.2m underspend; £11.3m budget vs £8.1m actual
findings.quote: The underspend is due in part to the rephasing of works at Farmstead Drive which are due to be completed later in 2026 and underspends on the Better Care Fund.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: A historic Dartford Rural legal claim required an additional £105,000 provision because the original estimate was insufficient
findings.detail: The council had made a provision for a historic legal claim, but discovered the provision was inadequate, requiring a further £105,000 draw from reserves. This reveals both a contingent liability and a reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Provisions that blow past their estimate suggest either weak risk assessment, hidden exposures, or poor claims management. A lender will want to know if there are other historic claims lurking.
findings.figures: £105,000 additional cost above original provision
findings.quote: Legal costs Dartford Rural Claim – a provision has been made regarding a historic legal claim. However this provision is not sufficient resulting in additional cost in the year of £105,000.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Planning appeals cost £138,000 in unbudgeted expenditure, funded from reserves
findings.detail: The council incurred £138,000 in planning appeal costs that were not anticipated in the budget. These were considered exceptional and funded from the Budget Stabilisation Reserve, indicating a spike in contested planning decisions or legal challenges.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted planning appeal costs point to either reputational/legal risk in the council's planning decisions or a shift in development pressure. A lender will want to know if this is one-off or a new baseline.
findings.figures: £138,000 unbudgeted expenditure
findings.quote: Planning appeals – This unbudgeted expenditure is forecast to cost in the region of £138,000. Due to the nature of the cost it has been identified to be funded from reserves.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Building Control revenues fell short and contractor costs exceeded budget, leaving a £230,000 gap
findings.detail: Building Control's fee income came in below forecast (demand or pricing issue), whilst staff and contractor costs overran, compounded by additional audit fees. This is the third-largest service overspend and suggests either the fee-setting model does not cover delivery costs or the service is under commercial pressure.
findings.matters: A statutory service running at a loss or below its cost recovery point signals either weak demand for the area's construction activity, pricing that the market will not bear, or poor cost control. Any could matter to a lender.
findings.figures: £230,000 unfavourable variance
findings.quote: Building control has an unfavourable variance of £230,000 due to lower than budgeted fee income and overspends due to additional costs of staff and contractors and additional audit fees.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Refuse Collection overspent by £293,000, driven by agency staff costs that salary underspends could not offset
findings.detail: The council's waste service cost £293,000 more than budgeted. The overspend is driven by agency staffing—a direct cost-control issue—and while some salary vacancies helped absorb the excess, they were not enough. This suggests the council is unable to recruit to budgeted establishment.
findings.matters: A lender sees a critical service (waste collection) running at higher cost than the council anticipated, with the council resorting to agency staff. This signals either understaffed budgets, recruitment failure, or poor cost control.
findings.figures: £293,000 unfavourable variance
findings.quote: Refuse collection has an unfavourable variance of £293,000 resulting from agency spend partially offset by salary underspends.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Cabinet ended the Commercial Trade Waste service after finding it unviable under new legislation
findings.detail: The council has ceased a trading service entirely due to ongoing challenges and forthcoming government legislation. The service forecasted a £188,000 loss this year and was judged unsustainable, signalling both current losses and an expectation of structural pressure ahead.
findings.matters: Service closures matter to a lender because they often indicate that the council cannot compete or is unable to adapt a line of business to regulatory change. It also confirms a material revenue stream is gone.
findings.figures: £188,000 unfavourable variance; service ended June 2025
findings.quote: Cabinet on 12 June 2025 approved this service to end due to the ongoing challenges and upcoming changes to government legislation which result in the service being unviable. This was forecast to be a £188,000 unfavourable variance.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Financial Monitoring Report - Draft Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Revenues and Benefits has lost government grant funding, creating a £463,000 structural overspend
findings.detail: The largest single departmental variance stems from previously received grants being stopped and reduced reserves. This is not a one-off; it indicates an ongoing funding gap the council will face in future years unless the gap is filled from elsewhere.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether core service funding is stable. Loss of grant revenue that does not return is a structural deterioration in the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £463,000 unfavourable variance
findings.quote: Revenues and Benefits are reporting an unfavourable variance of £463,000. This is partially due to previously received grants being stopped and reduced levels of reserves.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Consolidated Outturn Commentary 2025-26 Appendix A
findings.headline: Trade Waste service ceased in September
findings.detail: The council terminated its Trade Waste service in September 2025 as agreed by members. Finishing service expenses such as collecting bins increased the adverse forecast during wind-down, but the service no longer generates ongoing revenue.
findings.matters: Loss of a revenue-generating service reduces the council's income base and may indicate either market weakness or strategic decision to exit a non-core activity.
findings.figures: Trade Waste service stopped September 2025
findings.quote: As agreed by members, the service stopped in September. Finishing service expenses (such as collecting bins) has increased the adverse forecast.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Consolidated Outturn Commentary 2025-26 Appendix A
findings.headline: Swanley market contractor facing economic headwinds, council concedes on rent income
findings.detail: The Swanley market contractor is struggling with current economic conditions. Rather than enforcing the full contractual rent, the council has agreed to a temporary reduction in rent to support the contractor's viability. This represents a deliberate sacrifice of income to preserve the service.
findings.matters: Market contractor distress and the council's willingness to reduce expected income suggests weakness in local economic activity and reduces projected revenues.
findings.figures: £85k variance; temporary rent reduction agreed
findings.quote: The Swanley market contractor is finding the current economic conditions challenging. They are working hard to try and reverse the current difficult trading conditions. In the meantime the council has agreed to a temporary reduction in rent.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Consolidated Outturn Commentary 2025-26 Appendix A
findings.headline: Refuse collection overspent by £288k driven by high agency costs and £105k in sickness-related expenses
findings.detail: Waste collection costs exceeded budget by £288k due to high quantities of waste continuing, combined with agency staff costs caused by vacancies and absences. Sickness costs alone accounted for £105k of the overspend. Additional vehicle hire costs were incurred to replace a vehicle no longer usable.
findings.matters: Structural staffing pressures and high sickness absence signal potential workforce issues and indicate the council's waste management costs are unsustainable at current service levels.
findings.figures: £288k overspend; £105k of sickness costs; vehicle hire costs for replacement vehicle
findings.quote: High quantities of waste and recycling still continue. Agency costs are high due to staff vacancies and absences. The variance includes £105,000 of sickness costs.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Consolidated Outturn Commentary 2025-26 Appendix A
findings.headline: Building Control service underperformance with income significantly below budget, forcing contractor use and triggering fees review
findings.detail: Building Control fee income fell £230k short of budget due to market forces. The council has responded by bringing in contractors to cover vacant posts and has triggered an early review of fees and charges. The February forecast predicted a £19k underspend, but actual outturn showed a £24k overspend, indicating deteriorating conditions during the year.
findings.matters: A significant shortfall in a fee-earning service indicates market weakness and requires fee increases to recover, which may impact demand and the council's competitiveness.
findings.figures: £230k overspend; income currently behind budget profile; variance of £44k between February forecast and final outturn
findings.quote: Building Control Fee Income currently behind budget profile. Additional staffing costs, contractors covering vacant posts. The current situation has triggered an early review of fees and charges.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Consolidated Outturn Commentary 2025-26 Appendix A
findings.headline: Structural income loss from government grant transitions in council tax and benefits services
findings.detail: The council lost the Local Council Tax Support Grant (£111k) and multiple Council Tax Reduction Schemes grants, which previously offset expenditure. These losses, combined with the subsidy reserve no longer being available due to Universal Credit transition, created a £325k overspend in Benefits Admin and £139k in Local Tax services. Both services now lack the government funding that previously covered these costs.
findings.matters: Permanent loss of recurring grant income reduces the council's financial flexibility and may require service cuts or cost recovery through fees to offset.
findings.figures: £111k grant loss in Benefits Admin; £325k overspend in Benefits Admin; £139k overspend in Local Tax; multiple named grants lost (Council Tax Reduction Schemes Administration Grant, Incentives Grant, Empty Property Discounts & Premiums Grant)
findings.quote: Local Council Tax Support Grant £111K previously funded from Government, no longer received. Subsidy reserve previously used to offset expenditure no longer available due to transition to Universal Credit.

findings.paper_title: 06b Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Draft
findings.headline: Internal borrowing strategy depleting investment reserves and reducing investment income
findings.detail: Rather than external borrowing, the council has been using cash reserves to fund capital expenditure. This approach reduces available investment balances (from £11.3m to £15.4m over the recent period) and the income earned from those investments. The council proposes charging interest to internally-funded projects to offset this.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund capital reduces the council's financial buffer and liquidity, limiting its ability to absorb unexpected revenue pressures or manage cash flow timing issues.
findings.figures: Total treasury investments: £11,304k (31 March 2025), £15,382k (30 November 2025); External borrowing: £13,437k (30 November 2025)
findings.quote: However, this strategy results in a reduction in the level of investment balances the Council is able to hold and therefore reduces investment income. It is therefore proposed that interest may be charged against projects which are funded from internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 06b Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Draft
findings.headline: Planned major increase in external debt from £10.8m to £23.6m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council plans to increase external borrowing by £12.8m in 2026/27, nearly tripling debt levels from the current position of £10.8m. This represents a strategic shift from the current under-borrowed position where reserves have been used to fund capital.
findings.matters: This substantial increase in debt obligations will materially increase the council's annual interest costs and changes its financial position, which affects both creditworthiness and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: External debt at 31 March 2026: £10,837k; expected change 2026/27: +£12,774k; projected 31 March 2027: £23,611k
findings.quote: The Authority is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: 06b Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Draft
findings.headline: Regeneration project requiring £13.3m of new external borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council identifies a regeneration project requiring £13.3m in external borrowing during 2026/27, with a further £8.7m planned for 2028/29. This appears as a separate line item in the external borrowing forecasts, distinct from service-related borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what capital is being borrowed for and assess the project's viability and expected returns from regeneration initiatives.
findings.figures: External borrowing for regeneration: £13,280k (2026/27), £0 (2027/28), £8,704k (2028/29)
findings.quote: External borrowing table: Regeneration ... 13,280 0 8,704

findings.paper_title: 06b Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Draft
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing substantially from £52.9m to £110.7m over five years
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (CFR) is projected to grow significantly from £52.9m in 2024/25 to £110.7m by 2028/29. This reflects ongoing capital expenditure that exceeds immediate funding from grants and receipts, requiring increased debt over time.
findings.matters: The growing CFR indicates the council's long-term liabilities are increasing significantly, which directly affects financial sustainability and debt servicing capacity.
findings.quote: The Authority is asked to approve the CFR projections below: ... Total CFR 52,882 ... 110,728

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - App K(iii) - Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council acknowledges specific property investment risks to income sustainability
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies risks in property investment: property values can fall, and changing economic conditions could cause tenant vacancies. The council states it will manage these through sound decision-making, expert advice, and investment principles requiring strong market intelligence.
findings.matters: If property returns are material to the council's finances, volatility in property values or tenant solvency poses material operational and income sustainability risk.
findings.figures: None provided in this strategy document
findings.quote: Property investment is not without risk as property values can fall as well as rise and changing economic conditions could cause tenants to leave properties remaining vacant.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - App K(iii) - Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council relying on commercial property investment to supplement reduced grant funding
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has faced funding reductions and is turning to commercial activities and property investment to supplement its income and support service delivery. The Property Investment Strategy will guide these decisions within a formal governance framework.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand if the council's operating model depends on volatile commercial property returns rather than stable grant funding and the sustainability of this approach.
findings.figures: None provided in this strategy document
findings.quote: With reductions in funding that the Council has faced, it is having to look at commercial activities and property investment to supplement its income and support service delivery.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: 3-year budget relies on £92k drawdown from Budget Stabilisation Reserve to balance, with inflation risks not fully funded
findings.detail: Despite presenting a 'balanced budget', the 3-year plan shows a deficit of £92,000 (£31,000 per year) that is funded from the Budget Stabilisation Reserve. Additionally, inflation assumptions are below actual inflation and managers are instructed to absorb the gap within cash limits.
findings.matters: This indicates the council is running a structural small deficit that it is managing through reserve drawdown and spending discipline, rather than true balance. It leaves less headroom for shocks.
findings.figures: £92k 3-year deficit; £31k average annual drawdown; minimum reserve floor 10% (£2.3m for 2026/27)
findings.quote: The 3-year budget (Appendix Ci) shows a small deficit of £92,000 (£31,000 per year) which can be funded from the Budget Stabilisation Reserve resulting in a balanced budget position.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will cost further £1m over 2026/27 and 2027/28; full scope unclear
findings.detail: The council previously set aside £209k revenue budget and £200k reserve for LGR transition. It now proposes a further £1m to be split across 2026/27 and 2027/28. The report acknowledges significant costs are required 'from experience of other councils' but the precise scope remains unclear.
findings.matters: This is a material one-off cost to manage a transition of unknown scope. The fact that costs are being revised upward and further amounts flagged as likely suggests the council is still discovering the full bill.
findings.figures: £1m proposed 2026-28; prior £209k revenue + £200k reserve
findings.quote: In the 2025/26 budget process, a revenue budget of £209,000 was set up for this purpose together with a reserve of £200,000. In this budget a further amount of £1m is currently proposed to be split between 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: Non-pay inflation budgeted at 2.25% but actual inflation 3.2%; managers told to absorb the gap
findings.detail: The budget assumes non-pay costs will increase by an average of 2.25% annually. Actual CPI inflation stands at 3.2% (as of November 2025). The report notes that inflation has 'often been higher' than budget assumption in recent years and that service managers are expected to 'manage within their overall cash limit'.
findings.matters: This is a recipe for hidden overspends if managers cannot absorb the 0.95% annual gap. The council is essentially under-budgeting inflationary pressure and relying on services to absorb it.
findings.figures: 2.25% budget inflation assumption vs 3.2% CPI (November 2025); 0.95 percentage point gap
findings.quote: the budget assumes non-pay costs will increase by an average of 2.25% in all years. In practice, inflation has often been higher than this in recent years therefore it is up to managers to manage within their overall cash limit.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: National Insurance compensation covers only 42% of actual cost; £233k structural funding gap each year
findings.detail: The Employers National Insurance Contributions increase costs this council £404,000 annually. Government compensation (now rolled into Revenue Support Grant) covers only £171,000, leaving a £233,000 annual structural shortfall.
findings.matters: This is a recurring annual gap between statutory cost and government compensation. It does not resolve itself and grows with pay bills.
findings.figures: £404k cost; £171k compensation; £233k annual gap
findings.quote: The cost of the Employers National Insurance Contributions increase to this council is £404,000. This council received £171,000 in 2025/26 which is £233,000 below the expected cost.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: Council Tax base growth assumption slashed from 730 to 97 properties per annum, signalling slower housing delivery
findings.detail: The previous budget assumed Council Tax base would grow by 730 Band D equivalent properties annually, based on housing needs assessment. Actual growth in recent years has been only 97 properties. The budget has been revised to assume this lower rate for all three years ahead.
findings.matters: This is a significant downward revision to income growth, indicating the council's housing delivery has fallen far short of pre-existing projections. It signals either planning constraints, developer delays, or reduced household formation in the district.
findings.figures: 730 Band D properties assumed → 97 actual annual increase; three-year impact roughly £1.4m cumulative
findings.quote: The assumption in the budget approved in February was an increase of 730 Band D equivalent properties per annum. This was based on the pre-existing housing needs assessment. The actual increase in recent years has been much lower. The latest figures show the most recent annual increase of only 97 therefore the next three years have been changed to match this.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: Business Rates reset impact unknown; £2.6m of budget income depends on outcome still not determined
findings.detail: The Government committed to reset the business rates baseline for 2026/27. The council collects £45m in business rates but will retain £2.6m under the current scheme. The report states the full impact of the reset is not yet known. The council also decided not to set up its Business Rates Pool for 2026/27 due to the uncertainty, forgoing a potential retention benefit.
findings.matters: This is a major income line (£2.6m annually) with material uncertainty built into the budget assumptions. The decision not to pool suggests the council is bracing for a negative reset outcome.
findings.figures: £2.6m Business Rates income 2026/27; £45m gross business rates collected
findings.quote: A Business Rates reset has been due to take place for several years, but the Government has now committed to reset the baseline for retained business rates in full for 2026/27. The full impact of the reset is not yet known.

findings.paper_title: 06 - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 report CABINET
findings.headline: Pay award still unresolved; budget assumes 3% but unions demanding up to 10% on a £22m pay bill
findings.detail: Pay costs total £22m. The 2026/27 pay award negotiations have not been completed as of the report date. The National Employers and unions are in dispute, with the NJC unions requesting at least £3,000 or 10% (whichever is greater). The budget has been increased from 2% to 3% assumption, but if the union claim succeeds the shortfall could be material.
findings.matters: Pay is the council's largest cost item; a 10% award versus 3% budgeted would cost roughly £1.5m annually, creating a significant risk to the balanced budget claim.
findings.figures: £22m pay costs; 3% assumed in budget; unions demanding at least £3,000 or 10% whichever greater
findings.quote: Negotiations regarding the 2026/27 pay award have not been completed however, the NJC unions have requested an increase of at least £3,000 or 10% (whichever is greater) The assumption in the 3-year budget was originally a 2% annual increase, but this has been increased to 3%.

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register December 2025
findings.headline: Multiple control weaknesses in procurement, business continuity, and contract management increase governance risk
findings.detail: Internal audits have given 'Limited' assurance opinions on Procurement (August 2023), Business Continuity (November 2025), Contract Management (October 2023), and Health & Safety (September 2024). These Limited ratings indicate that controls in place are not sufficiently effective. Legal, Regulation & Procurement risk is scored at 12 (outside appetite). An action to implement the last procurement audit finding is overdue (due April 2026).
findings.matters: Limited audit assurance ratings across multiple control areas suggest the council's ability to execute procurement, manage contracts, and maintain continuity is weaker than necessary; this affects project delivery and financial reliability.
findings.figures: Four Limited assurance audit opinions; Legal risk score 12; last procurement audit action due April 2026
findings.quote: Internal Audit of Procurement (Limited - issued Aug 2023); Internal audit of Business Continuity (Issued – November 2025 Limited assurance)

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register December 2025
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates financial uncertainty while the council allocates budget for transition costs with no clear endpoint
findings.detail: The register identifies 'Insufficient financial resource allocated to the reorganisation process through additional government funding or the budget setting process' as a cause. The council's budget process has been amended to a 3-year balanced budget approach 'to reflect LGR and 3 year settlement'. LGR risk is scored at 12 (outside appetite) and unchanged for four quarters. Effects include 'Financial implications – additional cost associated with reorganisation' and 'Capital project delivery delays'.
findings.matters: LGR could materially change the council's structure, finances, and service configuration; planning multi-year borrowing or investment under this uncertainty is problematic for lenders.
findings.figures: LGR risk score: 12 (unchanged since March 2025)
findings.quote: Insufficient financial resource allocated to the reorganisation process through additional government funding or the budget setting process; Financial implications – additional cost associated with reorganisation

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register December 2025
findings.headline: The disposals programme is a critical bottleneck for capital funding and its delay threatens project delivery
findings.detail: The register lists 'Disposals programme not approved, impacting ability to raise capital funding and deliver capital programme' as a specific cause of capital project risk. A Disposals Policy was only adopted in April 2025. The council depends on selling surplus assets to fund capital investment, and delays to disposals cascade into project delays.
findings.matters: If the council cannot execute asset disposals on schedule, capital projects are delayed and potentially cancelled; this affects economic contribution and asset utilisation.
findings.figures: Disposals Policy adopted April 2025
findings.quote: Disposals programme not approved, impacting ability to raise capital funding and deliver capital programme

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register December 2025
findings.headline: Capital project delivery is at risk from inflation, material costs, and constrained funding sources
findings.detail: The council faces 'Economic conditions - higher than assumed inflation levels, high costs of building materials and skilled labour' while simultaneously struggling with 'Lack of available funding to deliver planned schemes either due to accessibility or acceptable interest rates'. The register notes that projects going over budget mean 'resources are diverted from other areas'. Capital delivery has a residual risk score of 12 and is outside appetite.
findings.matters: Capital projects overrunning creates revenue budget pressure; lenders need to understand whether capital commitments are at risk of cascading into revenue deficits.
findings.figures: Residual risk score on capital delivery: 12 (unchanged for four quarters)
findings.quote: Economic conditions - higher than assumed inflation levels, high costs of building materials and skilled labour; Lack of available funding to deliver planned schemes either due to accessibility or acceptable interest rates

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register December 2025
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion on the council's annual accounts creates uncertainty about financial position
findings.detail: The council's annual accounts have received a disclaimed audit opinion, meaning the external auditor could not provide full verification of the council's financial position. This is listed as a cause of the council's budget delivery risk. The register notes this creates 'Reduced certainty of historic financial data' as an effect.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion signals material uncertainty about the council's actual financial health, which directly affects creditworthiness and lender confidence.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinion status noted; specific financial impact not quantified
findings.quote: Disclaimed opinion of the annual accounts

findings.paper_title: 07 - Treasury Management Mid Year Report v3
findings.headline: Capital programme is under active review and subject to revision due to inflationary pressure and supply-chain constraints, creating uncertainty in final borrowing need.
findings.detail: The council states that its £29.779m capital programme 'is being kept under review due to the effects of inflationary pressure, shortages of materials and labour'. The council signals that its 'borrowing strategy will, therefore, also be regularly reviewed and revised, if necessary, to achieve the progression of the Capital Programme.' This indicates the current revised budget and borrowing forecasts may not be final, and the council may revise both downward if projects cannot proceed, or upward if inflation pushes costs higher.
findings.matters: A capital programme and borrowing forecast that is actively under review creates uncertainty for lenders evaluating the council's medium-term debt trajectory. Execution risk on £29.779m of capital spending means the £20.421m borrowing forecast is contingent on programme delivery that the council itself does not yet regard as certain.
findings.figures: £29.779m revised capital programme subject to review; inflation and supply constraints currently constraining delivery
findings.quote: The capital programme is being kept under review due to the effects of inflationary pressure, shortages of materials and labour. Our borrowing strategy will, therefore, also be regularly reviewed and revised, if necessary, to achieve the progression of the Capital Programme.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Treasury Management Mid Year Report v3
findings.headline: Council is deferring borrowing despite a £72.615m underlying capital financing requirement and plans to enter the market later in the year.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying need to borrow for capital) stands at £72.615m, up from £59.006m originally. However, actual external borrowings remain just £14.514m. The council states it is using cash flow in lieu of borrowing as 'prudent and cost-effective in the current economic climate' but notes this 'will require ongoing monitoring if gilt yields remain elevated'. The council explicitly states 'It is anticipated that further borrowing may be undertaken during this financial year subject to the progression of the Capital Programme.'
findings.matters: The council is timing a £57m+ borrowing entry into the market later in the year, creating concentration and timing risk. If gilt yields remain elevated or deteriorate, the council could face significantly higher interest costs than it would have incurred by borrowing earlier at lower rates, or face market access issues if conditions tighten.
findings.figures: CFR £72.615m vs actual borrowings £14.514m; Borrowing headroom of £58.1m unfunded; Operational boundary estimate for borrowing £60.0m
findings.quote: Despite the overall financial position and the underlying need to borrow for capital purposes (the CFR), no new external borrowing has been undertaken. It is anticipated that further borrowing may be undertaken during this financial year subject to the progression of the Capital Programme.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Treasury Management Mid Year Report v3
findings.headline: Capital programme increased 44% to £29.779m with borrowing requirement more than doubling to £20.421m, after capital receipts fell short by £7.8m.
findings.detail: The capital expenditure budget was revised upward from £20.732m to £29.779m, driven by approval of the Waste and Recycling Strategy in the Finance and Trading directorate. To finance this £9.4m increase, the council expected to draw on capital receipts, but actual receipts collapsed from £10.118m to £2.300m. Combined with a £9.4m spending increase, the shortfall in receipts forced the borrowing requirement from £8.286m to £20.421m.
findings.matters: A 44% capital spending increase coupled with a significant shortfall in capital receipts (a 77% drop from forecast) signals that the council's asset disposal strategy or capital receipts generation is underperforming. The council must now borrow substantially to fund plans it expected to self-finance, materially changing its debt trajectory.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £20.732m to £29.779m; Borrowing requirement £8.286m to £20.421m; Capital receipts £10.118m to £2.300m
findings.quote: The increase in Finance and Trading is due to the approval of the Waste and Recycling Strategy.
